idiom_name: hand-written wrapper struct implementing the trait + Arc<AtomicBool> revocation flag
implementation_notes: Rust has neither reflection nor proxy objects, so the forwarder is a struct that implements the target's trait, holds a clone of the shared target (Arc<Target>) and a shared flag (Arc<AtomicBool>), and checks the flag in every method before forwarding. Sharing is what makes revocation possible at all - a plain bool behind a shared reference cannot be flipped - and the atomic's Ordering is what makes the revoker's store visible to calling threads; revoking is a store of false on the same Arc. When the policy is drain rather than fail-fast, guard the grant with std::sync::RwLock and have the revoker take the write guard so it blocks until every in-flight call has released its read guard. There is no library-provided version; the structure is hand-written once per trait.
pitfalls: The flag must be shared and read with a synchronizing Ordering: a bool owned by the wrapper cannot be flipped through &self, and a Relaxed load gives no ordering for the data the call then touches, so the flag and the target need an Acquire/Release pair (or a Mutex).

Holding Arc<Session> keeps the target alive for the forwarder's lifetime; if revocation should also end the target's life, hold Weak and upgrade per call - and decide what a failed upgrade returns instead of panicking.
RwLock-based draining cannot span await points and the lock is poisoned when a writer panics, so the drain variant must choose how to recover rather than unwrapping the poisoned result.
